newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Trichet wants consensus on rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Trichet wants consensus on rates.

text.p: Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet has called for consensus on French monetary policy, warning that a vehement domestic debate could be damaging, according to minutes of a parliamentary finance committee hearing released on Thursday.

He told the committee, which held a closed-door hearing with Trichet on Wednesday, that market rates were set by international capital markets and the Bank's Monetary Policy Council did not have an automatic lever to lower them.
"He deduced from that that too 'vehement' a domestic debate on French monetary policy was immediately projected abroad and was paid for in terms of interest rates," the minutes said.

"He emphasised that the strengthening of a wide political consensus on the conduct of monetary policy would be more helpful to the Bank of France, whose role is to help our country benefit from market interest rates which are as low as possible," the minutes quoted him as saying.
The independent Bank of France has come under fire from some politicians for failing to cut rates fast enough in the face of weak economic growth.

President Jacques Chirac said in July that interest rates should fall further, sparking financial market worries about a rift between the government and the Bank of France and putting pressure on the franc.
Trichet ruled out any depreciation of the franc, which he said would lead to higher interest rates.
"...it was completely contradictory to want at the same time a weak currency and low interest rates," he was quoted as saying.
He said interest rates supported growth and that conditions for a return to growth were in place, on condition there was a pyschological lift and recovery in investment.
Trichet also told the finance committee that he was convinced that France would meet Maastricht treaty criteria for entry into a single currency in 1999.
The government presents a 1997 budget next week designed to ensure that France meets Maastricht standards on budget deficits.
He said the credibility of the European single currency would be supported by the stabilty of exchange rates between seven countries in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
"As regards entry to the single currency, he said he hoped the biggest number of countries possible could be in the first 'train'," the minutes quoted him as saying.

But in the absence of appropriate reduction in inflation differentials, the single currency could create serious difficulties in terms of competitiveness, while France. Germany and the Netherlands would suffer the reverse effect of higher interest rates due to the damage to the euro's credibility.

"He insisted on the fact that the credibility of the single currency was largely supported by the stability seen for nine and a half years in exchange rates of seven countries in the European Monetary System Exchange Rate Mechanism (France, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Denmark and Austria)," the minutes said.

As regards the lira, this had partly corrected its sharp depreciation since it left the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) after a currency crisis in 1992. Italy is now seeking to bring it back into the ERM.
"Mr Jean-Claude Trichet indicated that the appreciation in the lira had been substantial in recent months and had partly corrected the excesses of the previous depreciation," the minutes said.
Countries wanting to join monetary union when it is first launched in 1999 must prove their currencies have been stable for the last two years.
